deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics by Riemann: no derivation, computation or marginal note is visible. It is a printed page (p. 384) from the Göttingen Royal Society of Sciences' annual report, almost certainly the Nachrichten von der K. Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften of December 1863. Judging by p. 385, it was printed in Fraktur before the Nachrichten switched to Latin type in 1864, and it sits among Riemann's papers in the bundle 'R.Primzahlen' (Bl. 15v).

(1) The page finishes the physical class's botanical prize question on the germination and spore function of Lycopodium and its affinity among the vascular cryptogams, which was set for November 1863. It records that the question found no entrant and is reset for November 1866.

(2) It then announces the mathematical class's prize question for November 1864, in Latin and in German. Modern restatement: tables of primes keep showing pairs (p, p+2) with both p and p+2 prime, so it is 'very probable' that this sequence never stops. The Society asks for a rigorous proof ('argumentis firmis' / 'strenge Schlüsse') deciding whether the set {p : p and p+2 both prime} is infinite or not. That is, the twin prime problem: decide whether pi_2(x) -> infinity.

The empirical premise is the only 'reasoning' on the page. That premise is that twin primes persist in tables as far as they go (e.g. pi_2(10^3) = 35, pi_2(10^4) = 205).

The next page states a prize of 50 ducats, with submissions due by the end of September of the year concerned. Riemann was a member of the Göttingen mathematical class at this time. His keeping this clipping in his prime-number papers suggests his interest in, and plausibly involvement with, the question. The page itself does not show authorship, though. The problem is open to this day (best result: bounded gaps, Zhang 2013 / Maynard–Tao, gap <= 246).
errors: No mathematical errors; the page is a printed problem statement, not a derivation. Calling the infinitude 'valde verisimile' on numerical grounds is a heuristic, which the text correctly marks as unproven.

results.what: Official 1863 prize question of the Göttingen Royal Society (mathematical class) for November 1864: decide rigorously whether there are infinitely many twin primes
results.usually_credited_to: Alphonse de Polignac (1849, general prime-gap conjecture); folklore earlier; quantitative form Hardy–Littlewood 1923

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed public prize announcement, not a manuscript result. The Göttingen twin-prime prize question is a known if minor historical fact. Its presence in Riemann's prime-number Nachlass hints at his role in posing it, which is a mildly interesting historical detail but contains no new mathematics.

transcription_corrections: The Latin line break reads 'quo-' / 'quousque pergitur' in the print. The printed text thus has the doubled 'quo-quousque', which is a typesetting duplication; the intended word is 'quousque'. The machine transcription faithfully reproduces this as 'quoquousque'.
The transcription matches the image otherwise. The page is printed Fraktur and Antiqua, not Riemann's handwriting, and there are no handwritten annotations to transcribe.
On the next page, 'K. Gellschaft' should be 'K. Gesellschaft' (this may be a misprint in the original).
